title: The Destruction of Łuków’s Jewish Community
summary: The memorial book’s defining account is the destruction of the people and communal world it seeks to preserve.

## A town under attack

For Łuków’s Jews, destruction did not begin with a single deportation. It unfolded through invasion, killings, forced labor, confinement and successive actions that brought Jews from nearby towns into the same trap. Before the war, about 6,200 Jews lived in Łuków—roughly half the population—and the community sustained religious, charitable, political and cultural institutions. The wider record describes both an established local community and a regional hub that would become a gathering point for Jews displaced from elsewhere. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=529))

The memorial book’s accounts of September 1939 do not give one tidy sequence. They recall German attacks, shootings, houses burning and residents fleeing; separate entries date shootings to September 16 and German violence to September 18. Yad Vashem dates the German occupation of Łuków to September 19, when Jews were killed and homes burned. These accounts may refer to events across several days, but the records do not let us resolve every date or detail. The book’s image of a town burning is testimony to local catastrophe, not a complete operational chronology. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/lukow/lukow.html?utm_source=openai))

German rule brought new coercion quickly. A book record describes an order in early 1940 compelling Jewish men aged sixteen to sixty to perform forced labor. Yad Vashem gives a broader age range—twelve to sixty—and says that many Jews were compelled to work in Łuków, nearby labor camps or farther away in the Lublin district. The differing ages should not be collapsed into one figure: they may describe different orders or recollections. In 1940, a ghetto was established; in May 1941, the German authorities formed the ghetto described by Virtual Shtetl, encompassing several street clusters. By November, leaving the designated area was punishable by death. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=529))

## Confinement, labor and the changing population

The ghetto was not only a place of confinement but a mechanism for exploitation. Virtual Shtetl describes overcrowding, inadequate sanitation, hunger and forced labor. The memorial book likewise remembers labor orders and the precarious status of those classified as workers. Even a work assignment offered no security: it made a person temporarily useful to German authorities, not safe from later murder or deportation. ([sztetl.org.pl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/l/729-lukow/116-sites-of-martyrdom/48334-getto-w-lukowie))

The population under occupation was never simply the prewar community. Yad Vashem reports that Jews from other Polish towns were brought to Łuków from 1939 onward, and that about 2,000 Jews from Slovakia arrived in the first half of 1942. By May 1942, it estimates the ghetto population at 10,000. Later, Jews from nearby localities—including Adamów, Kock, Stanin and Tuchowicz—were also forced into Łuków. These movements enlarged the community’s suffering while making the ghetto a regional staging point for deportation. They also mean that a story of Łuków’s destruction includes people whose homes had been elsewhere. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=529))

The book’s witnesses remember violence before the mass deportations as well as during them. One account describes the Gestapo arrest and beating of Sonye; another recalls shootings during roundups and people being taken from hiding places. The fragments supplied here do not provide enough detail to reconstruct Sonye’s family or her eventual fate, and the name alone cannot safely identify her in other records. Her experience belongs to a wider pattern in which arrest, beating and forced movement were part of daily terror, not only a prelude to the October actions. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/lukow/lukow.html?utm_source=openai))

## October 1942: the ghetto is emptied by stages

The book preserves memories of encirclement, gunfire, orders to assemble and Jews driven toward the station. One witness recalls German, Ukrainian and Latvian forces surrounding the town, searching homes and shooting people found in hiding. The memorial book’s account also describes Jews forced to lie face down in the market square, older people separated and killed, and others marched to the railway. Such testimony restores the human experience of the roundup: families had to choose in moments whether to obey, hide or try to flee. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/lukow/luk505.html))

The wider record helps establish the scale and sequence, while showing that no single number covers every stage. Yad Vashem dates a major action to October 5, 1942, and reports about 5,000 deported to Treblinka and about 2,000 Jews murdered outside the town. It records further deportations on November 7–8, with thousands sent to Treblinka and about 200 killed at the Jewish cemetery. Virtual Shtetl likewise describes the October roundup, the deportation of thousands and the arrival of people from nearby communities later that month. The book’s connected entries describe encirclement on October 1 and an Aktion without an exact date; those references should not be mistaken for proof that all accounts describe the same day. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=529))

The name [Treblinka](/communities/lukow/records/mention_d0cc1f39b4d42e016c7b5345) was the destination named in the witnesses’ memories. The memorial book also records the terror of deportation itself: Jews marched under guard, loaded into railway cars and taken away. The outside record identifies Treblinka as the destination of the deportations. In the remaining ghetto, a smaller group of Jews was kept for labor, including work connected with German warehouses; the distinction between the deported and those temporarily retained did not mean the latter had escaped danger. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/lukow/luk505.html))

## The last transports—and the people who remained

After the October and November actions, Łuków’s Jewish population continued to include survivors of the roundups, forced laborers and Jews transferred from neighboring places. The records disagree in emphasis and sometimes in detail about the numbers killed locally and deported. Yad Vashem reports that hundreds remained legally while more than a thousand others had evaded deportation by the end of 1942; Virtual Shtetl describes a much smaller labor group. The discrepancy cautions against treating any one estimate as a complete count of everyone in hiding, at work or in transit. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=529))

A book entry gives May 2, 1942, as a date associated with the destruction of Jewish families, while another explicitly dates the liquidation of Jewish life to May 2, 1943. The latter year is consistent with Yad Vashem and Virtual Shtetl, both of which identify May 2, 1943, as the final liquidation. On that day, the ghetto was set alight; some Jews were shot at the cemetery and others deported to Treblinka. Sources give different estimates for the final group—about 1,500 murdered in Yad Vashem’s account and roughly 2,000–3,000 deported in Virtual Shtetl’s—so the figures should remain distinct rather than be forced into a false total. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=529))

But May 2, 1943, was not the end of danger for every person hiding in Łuków. The memorial book records the murder, on February 27, 1944, of people discovered in a bunker, including a father, a daughter and the narrator’s relatives. That account reminds us that liquidation did not instantly end the hunt for Jews who had survived by hiding. Nor does the memorial book’s surviving testimony encompass everyone: its voices are those of people able to survive, remember and write. Yad Vashem estimates that only a small number escaped to the forests; Virtual Shtetl reports about 150 survivors from Łuków and the displaced population. These figures use different frames, but both point to the near-total destruction of a community whose life had once filled the town’s streets and institutions. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/lukow/lukow.html?utm_source=openai))
